---
title: "Planned Factorial Analysis of Mixed Designs with Simple Effects"
output: rmarkdown::html_vignette
vignette: >
  %\VignetteIndexEntry{planned-factorial_mixed-designs_simple-effects}
  %\VignetteEngine{knitr::rmarkdown}
  %\VignetteEncoding{UTF-8}
---

A vignette to demonstrate how to conduct a planned analysis with simple effects contrasts of a between- x within-subjects design, using PsyR to generate Simultaneous Confidence Intervals (SCIs) pertaining to each defined contrast. Simple effects contrasts allow a researcher to analyse cell mean differences at one level of a factor by the level (or levels) of the other factor. This is relevant when trying to understand what may be driving an interaction effect, as an interaction effect contrast may be partitioned into two simple effects contrasts. Further, this vignette demonstrates analysis using a multivariate model, as within-subjects data necessarily violates assumptions of sphericity and as such must be analysed in a multivariate fashion.

In partitioning analysis out at the individual level of a factor, a simple effects analysis produces non-orthogonal families which are incompatible with how an ANOVA-F Simultaneous Test Procedure (STP) controls the Family Wise Error Rate (FWER). Instead, and as will be demonstrated in this vignette, a simple effects analysis may define a single non-standard all-factorial contrasts family, allowing for investigation of simple effects, main effects and interaction effects across all families.

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```
## The Packages

To use PsyR to calculate confidence intervals over contrast effects, we will utilise a workflow with functions from [afex](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/afex/versions/1.4-1) to implement ANOVA models, and [emmeans](https://rvlenth.github.io/emmeans/) to obtain estimated marginal means and the required contrast estimates. So let's load those packages, and any others that are helpful for our workflow.

```{r setup, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(afex)
library(emmeans)
library(PsyR)
library(tidyverse)
```

## The Data

The `depression` dataframe contains the results of a longitudinal study examining the impact of treatments for depression on *N* = 15 patients. Patients are randomly assigned to one of *J* = 3 treatment conditions (Treatment 1, Treatment 2, or a waitlist Control), and their happiness is measured at *p* = 3 occasions (pre-treatment, immediately post-treatment, and at a follow up). The dependent variable is happiness, with a higher score being indicative of greater happiness.

Let's load the data, then call the `head()` function to print the first 5 rows.

```{r loaddata}
data(depression)
head(depression, 5)
```

To learn more about the `depression` dataframe, call the help function using `?df` to open its documentation.

```{r, whatdepression, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, eval = FALSE}
?depression
```

Also, let's tidy up the data, labelling the levels of our independent variables for greater clarity.

```{r sortdep}
depression <- depression %>%
  mutate(
    Group = fct_relevel(Group, 'Ctrl', 'Tmt1', 'Tmt2'),
    Time = fct_relevel(Time, 'Pre', 'Post', 'FU'),
    Subject = factor(Subject)
  )
```

Next, let's visualise our data. Doing so allows us to more intuitively understand its layout.

```{r plothappiness,  fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
depression %>% 
  group_by(Group, Time) %>%
  summarise(mean_happiness = mean(Happiness)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Time, y = mean_happiness, group = Group, colour = Group)) +
  geom_point(aes(fill = Group, shape = Group), size = 3) +
  geom_line() + 
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(21:24)) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 14) +
  theme(legend.position = c(.15, .80))
```

## The Analysis

Here we will obtain and store the necessary output from which to use PsyR to generate SCIs.

To start, we must generate an ANOVA model of our data. To do so, let's specify that we want a multivariate analysis, using `afex::afex_options()`. Next, create a new object `mod` by calling `afex::aov_ez()`. `mod` will take in the `Subject` column to identify subjects, the `Happiness` column as the dependent variable, the `depression` dataframe, the `Group` column as the between-subjects factor, and the `Time` column as the within-subjects factor. Note that the generation and storage of this ANOVA model in this specific manner is essential for downstream compatibility with functions in the `emmeans` package, and for eventual generation of SCIs with PsyR.

```{r aov, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
afex_options(emmeans_model = "multivariate")

mod <- aov_ez(
  "Subject", 
  "Happiness", 
  depression, 
  between = "Group",
  within = "Time" 
)
```

Next, let's obtain cell means for each of the nine possible cells in our design. To do so, create a new object `emms`. Then, call `emmeans::emmeans()` and specify that we want to take in `mod` (the object we just made) and output based upon `Group` and `Time`. 

``` {r, emms_cell_means}
emms <- emmeans(mod, c("Group", "Time"))
```
``` {r, emms_cell_means_hidden, echo = FALSE}
emms |> 
  as.data.frame() |> 
  select(Group:df) |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

Time to define our contrasts!

Given this is a planned analysis, contrasts must be defined prior to data collection. In this example, the following between-subjects main effects contrasts are chosen for analysis:

- "Ts - Ctrl" ➞ The difference between the average happiness scores of Treatments 1 and 2 and the waitlist Control.

- "T1 - T2" ➞ The difference between the average happiness scores of Treatment 1 and Treatment 2.

```{r, btwn}
between_contrasts = list(
  "Ts - Ctrl" = c(-1, 0.5, 0.5),
  "T1 - T2" = c(0, 1, -1)
)
```

Now that we have defined our between-subjects main effects contrasts, let's obtain the row means for the between-subjects Group condition. To do so, create `emms_btwn` by calling `emmeans::emmeans()`, placing `mod` in the "object" argument and outputting based upon the between-subjects factor `Group`. 

``` {r, get_btwn_emms}
emms_btwn <- emmeans(mod, c("Group"))
```
``` {r, get_btwn_emms_hidden, echo = FALSE}
emms_btwn |> 
  as.data.frame() |> 
  select(Group:df) |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

Next, let's generate and store statistical output pertaining to our between-subjects main effects contrasts. To do so, create the `btwn_fx` object. Next, call `emmeans::contrast()`, setting `emms_grp` in the "Object" argument and `btwn_contrasts` in the "Method" argument.

```{r, getbtwnfx}
btwn_fx <- contrast(emms_btwn, between_contrasts)
```
```{r, kable_btwnfx, echo = FALSE}
btwn_fx |> 
  as.data.frame() |> 
  select(contrast:df) |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

Let's also define our within-subjects main effect contrasts. As with our between-subjects main effect contrasts, these must be defined prior to data collection. In this example, the following contrasts are chosen for analysis:

- "Post - Pre" ➞ The difference between average happiness scores taken post versus pre-treatment.

- "FU - Post" ➞ The difference between average happiness scores taken at follow-up versus post-treatment.

```{r, within}
within_contrasts = list(
  "Post - Pre" = c(-1, 1, 0),
  "FU - Post" = c(0, -1, 1)
)
```

Following similar steps as with our between-subjects contrasts, let's obtain the column means for the different time points of measurement and store the results of statistical output of the main effects contrasts in the `win_fx` object.

``` {r, emms_win}
emms_win <- emmeans(mod, "Time")
``` 
``` {r, emms_win_hidden, echo = FALSE}
emms_win |> 
  as.data.frame() |> 
  select(Time:df) |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

```{r wthn}
win_fx <- contrast(emms_win, within_contrasts)
```
```{r, kable_winfx, echo = FALSE}
win_fx |> 
  as.data.frame() |> 
  select(contrast:df) |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

Finally, let's obtain statistical output pertaining to our interaction contrasts. Note that our interaction contrasts will be the product of each combination of our between- and within-subjects main effects contrasts. 

To generate and store this output, create `int_fx` and call `emmeans::contrast()`. Place `emms` in the "Object" argument, and place a list of our between and within-subjects contrasts in the "Interaction" argument.

```{r int_fx}
int_fx <- contrast(
  emms, 
  interaction = list(between_contrasts, within_contrasts)
)
```
```{r, kable_intfx, echo = FALSE}
int_fx |> 
  as.data.frame() |> 
  select(Group_custom:df) |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

### Simple Effects

In this analysis, we will define a single all factorial family consisting of the A(b), B(a), A, B and AB effects. This will allow us to investigate both *a* and *b* simple effects. Note that if only one of *a* or *b* simple effects is of interest, it is also possible to define two factorial families, from which one can generate analysis with greater statistical power.

To obtain output pertaining to simple effects contrasts, we require the cell means from our data. While we had previously stored these within `emms`, the way in which they are stored in `emms` is incompatible with our later code. Instead, we must generate and store cell means as split by the `Group` column of our dataframe. To do so, create `win_by_grp` and call `emmeans::emmeans()`. Place `mod` in the "Object" argument, and `Time` by `Group` in the "Specs" argument. 

``` {r win_by_grp_emms}
win_by_grp <- emmeans(mod, ~ Time | Group)
```
``` {r win_by_grp_emms_hidden, echo = FALSE}
win_by_grp |> 
  as.data.frame() |>
  select(Time:df) |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

Next, let's generate statistical output pertaining to each cell in our design. To do so, create `win_by_grp_fx` and call `emmeans::contrast()`. Place our newly made `win_by_grp` in the "Object" argument and `within_contrasts` in the "Method" argument.

```{r, win_by_grp_fx}
win_by_grp_fx <- contrast(win_by_grp, method = within_contrasts)
```
```{r, kable_wingrp_fx, echo = FALSE}
win_by_grp_fx |> 
  as.data.frame() |> 
  select(contrast:df) |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

Let's now store output from which emmeans can compute simple effects contrasts related to our between-subjects main effects contrasts. To do so, call `base::list()` and define coefficient vectors which point to the "Post" and "FU" levels of our within-subjects factor.

Next, create the `win_sfx` object. Call `emmeans::contrast()`, placing `emms` in the "Object" argument and a list of our between-subjects and within-simple contrasts in the "Interaction" argument. This will allow emmeans to compute four simple effects contrasts pertaining to our between-subjects main effects contrasts at the cell levels of "post" and "FU".

```{r, btwn_at_within}
within_simple <-  list(
  "Post*" = c(0, 1, 0),
  "FU*" = c(0, 0, 1)
)
win_sfx <- contrast(emms, interaction = list(between_contrasts, within_simple))
```
```{r, kable_win, echo = FALSE}
win_sfx |> 
  as.data.frame() |> 
  select(Group_custom:df) |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

Following similar steps, let's generate and store statistical output of simple effects contrasts capturing differences between levels of the between-subjects factor for each within-subjects main effects contrast.

``` {r btwn_by_grp_emms}
btwn_by_grp <- emmeans(mod, ~ Group | Time)
```
``` {r btwn_by_grp_emms_hidden, echo = FALSE}
btwn_by_grp |> 
  as.data.frame() |>
  select(Group:df) |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 3) 
```

```{r, btwn_by_grp_fx}
btwn_by_grp_fx <- contrast(btwn_by_grp, method = between_contrasts)
```
```{r, kable_btwngrp_fx, echo = FALSE}
btwn_by_grp_fx |> 
  as.data.frame() |> 
  select(contrast:df) |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

```{r, btwn_simp_conts}
between_simple <-  list(
  "Ctrl*" = c(1, 0, 0),
  "T1*" = c(0, 1, 0),
  "T2*" = c(0, 0, 1)
)
btwn_sfx <- contrast(emms, interaction = list(within_contrasts, between_simple))
```
```{r, kable_btwntreat, echo = FALSE}
btwn_sfx |> 
  as.data.frame() |> 
  select(Group_custom:df) |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

### Applying PsyR to generate SCIs

To generate SCIs relevant to each contrast within our planned analysis, let's do the following. First, create the object `all_fx`, within which we will store a vector that contains statistical output pertaining to all contrasts of interest within our all factorial family. Next, create `alphas`, which will take in a list of alphas of $m$ length, where $m$ = 3 = the number of families in our analysis. Here, alpha will be set at $m · ⍺$ ($3 · .05 = .15$).

Next, we will call psyci() and input the following.

- The model is set as the previously made `mod` object, where the model must be made using the afex package (and of class afex_aov).

- The contrast_tables argument is set as the previously made `all_fx` list.

- The method is set as "bf" to indicate a Bonferonni adjustment should be enacted.

- Alpha is set at `alphas`, indicating the desired type I error rate should be set per family at .15 (as has been previously established).

- Note that while PsyR generally infers the family and participating factors for every original emmgrid, the family_group must be manually defined when conducting an all-factorial simple effects analysis. To do so, call `base::rep()` to generate the string "all_factorial" a number of times equal to the length of `all_fx` (3).

```{r, psyci}
all_fx <- c(win_fx, btwn_fx, int_fx, win_sfx, btwn_sfx)
alphas = 3*.05 # 3 * alpha / nk

output <- psyci(
  model = mod,
  contrast_tables = all_fx,
  method = "bf",
  alpha = alphas,
  family_group = rep("all_factorial", length(all_fx))
)
```
``` {r, kable_output, echo = FALSE}
display <- output %>%
  unclass() %>%
  bind_rows() %>%
  mutate(
   Group = coalesce(contrast, Group_custom),
   Time = coalesce(contrast, Time_custom),
  ) %>%
  select(estimate:F_value, p_value_adjusted, cc:upper, Group, Time) %>%
  relocate(Group, Time)

display[1, 1] <- NA
display[2, 1] <- NA
display[3, 2] <- NA
display[4, 2] <- NA

knitr::kable(display, digits = 3)
```

## The Interpretation

Simple Effects Contrasts are generally used to clarify what may be driving an interaction effect. To demonstrate this, let's examine the interaction between **T1 - T2 × FU - Post**, as well as its constituent simple effects contrasts.

This interaction contrast looks at how treatments 1 and 2 differentially impact happiness scores at follow-up versus immediately post treatment. As a first port of call, it is helpful to return to our visualisation of the data, which  shows that patients who received treatment 2 were happier at follow-up than those who received treatment 1. An examination of our interaction contrast shows this was significantly significant: patients who received treatment 2 were on average between 3.049 and 12.951 points happier at follow-up than at post as compared to those who received treatment 1. This interpretation, while correct, can be further clarified. Specifically, it would be useful to quantify whether this effect is driven by either the type of treatment or the time of measurement.

To understand what is driving the interaction, we may partition it into its two constituent simple effects contrasts: From these, we learn the following:

- T1 - T2 (Post) & T1 - T2 (FU): There is insufficient evidence of a significant difference between treatments at the post-treatment measure (-2.070, 6.070), and at the follow-up measure (-12.410, 0.410). 

- FU - Post (Tmt1) & FU - Post (Tmt2): Happiness scores in patients who received treatment 1 are between 4.499 and 11.501 points lower at follow-up as compared to post treatment. There is insufficient evidence of this effect in treatment 2, such that patients are just as happy at follow-up as at post-treatment (-3.501, 3.501).

### The Benefits of SCIs

In conducting a simple effects analysis with SCIs, we have been able to clarify our understanding of the T1 - T2 × FU - Post interaction effect. Specifically, we have shown that it is driven by the tendency of patients who received treatment 1 to experience significantly reduced happiness at follow-up as compared to immediately post-treatment.

Further, by examining the overlap (or lack thereof) between simple effects confidence intervals, one can infer differences at the population level. For example, the SCIs of the simple effects of Treatments 1 and 2 at follow-up versus immediately post-treatment allows us to infer that the respective population means are different, as the upper bound (-4.499) of FU - Post (Tmt1) does not overlap with the lower bound (-3.501) of FU - Post (Tmt 2).

Finally, SCIs are especially useful if thresholds of importance are introduced. For example, imagine that a difference of **3 dependent units** was deemed the smallest of clinical importance. In this case, the FU - Post (Tmt1) simple effects contrast is both significant and clinically important (as |-4.499| > 3). Likewise, the Ts - Ctrl (Post) simple effects contrast is significant, but may or may not be clinically important (as 2.475 < 3).

### Limitations of a Simple Effects Analysis

Engaging in a simple effects analysis, as compared to an analysis of just main and interaction effects, comes at the cost of reduced power.  This is necessarily the case because we are looking at cell means; in a between x within0subjects analysis, simple effects contrasts will necessarily have a reduced $n$ as compared to a main and interaction effects analysis.
